lines.text: A quarter of this country sits below sea level.
And it stays dry.
Not by luck. By centuries of engineering, and one terrible night in nineteen fifty three.
Zoom in on the lowest point in the Netherlands. It sits near the town of Nieuwerkerk aan den IJssel, about six point seven meters below sea level.
Stand a two storey house on that spot, and its roof would sit at sea level.
So how do you keep a town dry, when the ground is lower than the ocean?
Hey, I'm Jeremy. I'll be your guide through this one.
Meet the Netherlands. A country that has spent centuries arguing with water, and mostly winning.
Hi. Water is my whole thing.
Honestly, water and I have been roommates for centuries. We do not always get along.
Step one. Build a dike around a shallow lake or a salt marsh.
The first big one, the Beemster, was drained in sixteen twelve. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Step two. Pump the water out, and you get a polder. Dry land, below the water line, held in by walls.
For centuries, the pumps were windmills. The wind turned the sails, the sails turned the scoop wheel, and the water went up and over the dike.
Kinderdijk still has a row of those old windmills. You can walk right up to them.
The catch: peat soil shrinks as it dries, so the land sinks. The pumps never get a day off.
Stop pumping, and the lake comes back. It does not ask permission.
Some of the water boards that run this system are among the oldest democratic bodies in the country. A few date back to the thirteen hundreds.
In nineteen thirty two, they shut the sea out for good. The Afsluitdijk closed off the Zuiderzee, and it became the IJsselmeer, a lake.
That dam is more than thirty kilometers long, and it turned a sea arm into a freshwater lake.
Schiphol, the country's main airport, sits below sea level too. Planes land on reclaimed ground.
Oh, and I should introduce the North Sea. He has been waiting for his cue.
The North Sea is patient. Very patient. And very wet.
Then came the night of January thirty first, nineteen fifty three.
A storm surge drove the North Sea into the south west of the country. Dikes broke. Islands and polders flooded in hours.
Some families climbed into their attics to survive.
About eighteen hundred people died in the Netherlands. Around seventy thousand more were evacuated from their homes.
A government commission studied the disaster, and it recommended a complete plan.
After that night, the country made a promise. Never again.
The answer was the Delta Works. Dams and storm barriers that close off the sea arms.
The rule for the most populated western part of the country is strict: a flood chance of one in ten thousand a year.
Most of the time, the barriers stay open, and ships and tides pass through. When a storm surge comes, the gates close.
The Maeslant barrier is the famous one. Two huge steel gates that float on the water, and swing shut when the sea rises.
The Oosterschelde barrier went a different way. It stays open to the sea, so the mussel and oyster farms in the estuary kept their water.
Now picture a red line at sea level, cutting right through a town. That line is the threat. Everything the Dutch built is the answer.
Here is the twist. Engineers no longer design for the sea they remember.
They design for a sea that keeps rising.
Global sea level has risen about twenty centimeters since nineteen hundred.
Dutch planning now looks past the year twenty one hundred. Dikes get built with room to be raised later, so nobody has to start over.
Engineers call this adaptive planning. The plans get reviewed, and the numbers get updated, every few years.
The question changes. It is no longer, can we stop the sea? It is, how much room do we give it?
And this is the part I love. The Netherlands stopped only fighting the water, and started working with it.
Room for the River gives rivers more space to spread when they flood, instead of walls that grow higher every decade.
The Sand Motor is a giant sandbar, dumped into the sea. Waves and wind carry that sand along the coast for years.
In Rotterdam, a public square called the Benthemplein turns into a water basin when heavy rain falls.
Some homes in the country now float, rising and falling with the water, instead of being pumped dry.
A small country turned its biggest threat into its method.
So let me leave you with a question. If the sea came back for your town, what would you build first?
So, a quarter of this country sits below sea level. And it stays dry.
Not because the sea agreed to behave. Because people kept doing the math, and kept building.
